name: Beothuk
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Extinct; attested only via wordlists (e.g. Hewson's vocabularies); no stress description possible/found.

new_statements.quote: Too little information is on hand to establish any general rules for the accentuation. None of the accented words are oxytonized, but several have the antepenult emphasized : bashedtheek, ashwoging, dósomite ; the term ejabathook has the accent still further removed from the final syllable. Very likely the accent could in that language shift, as in other languages of America, from syllable to syllable, whenever rhetorical reasons required it. By some of the collectors the signs for length and brevity were used to designate the emphasized syllable, placed above or underneath the vowels.
new_statements.citation: Gatschet, Albert S. 1886. The Beothuk Indians. Second article. Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 23(123): 411-432.
new_statements.locator: pp. 418-419 (section on sounds; the paragraph begins on p. 418 and ends on p. 419)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (23-page JSTOR Early Journal Content scan, text layer present; PDF pages 9-10 = printed pp. 418-419, running heads 'Gatschet.] 418 [May 7,' and '1886.] 419 [Gatschet.'). The quoted paragraph is the last paragraph of p. 418 continuing to the top of p. 419, exactly at the stated locator, inside the sounds section (consonant table, remarks on lth/dr/dth/x, gemination, syllable structure) that precedes 'Alternation of sounds'. Rendered p. 418 to PNG and read it: printed text is 'Too little information is on hand to establish any general rules for the accentuation [italic]. None of the accented words are oxytonized, but several have the antepenult emphasized : báshedtheek, áshwoging, dóso…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule can be stated: the only evidence is accent marks on a handful of wordlist items. In those, stress is never on the final syllable and is often on the antepenult (or earlier), but the source declines to generalize.
new_statements.exceptions: Gatschet suggests the accent could shift from syllable to syllable for rhetorical reasons, as he believed of other American languages; he also warns that some collectors used length/brevity signs to mark the emphasized syllable, so the marks are ambiguous between stress and vowel length (Hewson 1978: 115 makes the same point and drops the marks).
new_statements.domain_note: Written wordlist forms (single words in citation form) with accent marks added by 19th-century English-speaking collectors; Gatschet never heard the language. No phrase-level observations.
new_statements.identity_note: Beothuk is extinct (last speaker Shanawdithit d. 1829); all data are 18th-19th-century English-orthography wordlists from Oubee, Demasduwit and Shanawdithit, compiled by Gatschet (1885-1890) and re-edited by Hewson (1978). No dialect issue; no other glottocode involved.

sources.note: pp. 418-419, in a section on sounds: too little information to establish general rules of accentuation; none of the accent-marked words are final-stressed, several show antepenult accent (bashedtheek, ashwoging, dosomite; ejabathook further from the end); accent probably mobile for rhetorical reasons; some collectors marked the emphasized syllable with length/brevity signs.
States there are practically no structural data for Beothuk; no phonology or stress section; used only to harvest references.
